decisive_wording: B opens with "Sustained 1.26M events/sec ... 1.2 µs per-message p99" and then gives the mechanism as "keeping each price level as a FIFO queue (std::list) inside a std::map, with an order-ID hash map for O(1) cancels"; A opens with "Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator"; C ends with "and a separate 2M-event run measured a 1.2 µs p99"
info_preserved_or_lost: All three keep the throughput, the p99, the separate 2M-event run, std::map plus std::list FIFOs, and O(1) cancels. A and C say what the hash map points to (list iterator / list node), which is why cancels are O(1). B drops that detail and says only "order-ID hash map". B uses "per-message" where A says "per-update" and C gives no unit.
credibility_change: A is the most exact about the mechanism, with the iterator mapping a senior engineer would check for. B is still credible because the parts it names give O(1) cancels. C is about as credible as A but tacks the latency on at the end, so it reads as an afterthought.
readability_change: B is easiest to read: the results come first, so a recruiter gets the numbers right away, and "FIFO queue (std::list) inside a std::map" is easy to follow. A opens with a dense stack of container names before any result. C is a run-on sentence with two "and" clauses and an awkward passive ending.

decisive_wording: "not a code change" and "do-nothing control book" (A) vs. "null control book" (B)
info_preserved_or_lost: Both keep the 1.65x figure, the CPU frequency governor root cause, perf counters, the control book, the drop in variance from about 6% to 0.06%, core pinning, and the fixed clock. Only A says outright that the code was not at fault, and A calls the slowdown a "regression".
credibility_change: A is slightly stronger. "not a code change" shows that a code cause was ruled out, which is the point of the debugging story and something a strong interview answer would cover. "Regression" is the standard engineering term.
readability_change: B is about six words shorter. A is easier to understand: a non-technical recruiter can restate "it wasn't the code, it was the CPU clock", and "do-nothing control book" is clearer than "null control book". A's extra words add meaning, not padding.
